BL-232.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31 (Ben, on seeing BL-231 land): "What do you think about bridging tiles with mountains? So for instance, three tiles in a line would have a wavy mountain marker, where a diamond might cover the entire interior."

## Why this is right

BL-231 put a glyph on each dramatic-landform tile independently, so a three-tile run draws the
same silhouette three times. Real maps do not do that — a range is drawn as ONE ridge crossing
however many tiles it occupies, and the shape of that ridge is the information. Repeating an
identical icon says "mountain here, mountain here, mountain here"; a spanning ridge says "this is
a range, and it runs this way".

This also recovers the thing BL-231's measurement talked us out of. That item planned an
edge/contour channel and dropped it because there is no continuous elevation gradient to contour
(95% of land is plains or valley). Spanning is the same idea aimed correctly: not contouring the
whole surface, but tracing the 1.5% that actually has a shape.

## THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS — reuse it, do not invent one

**BL-172's road span/symmetry fix, in this same file**, is exactly this problem already solved:
each roaded tile draws its OWN half of every shared road edge — from its centre to the MIDPOINT
of the centre-to-neighbour line — toward each roaded, survey-revealed cardinal neighbour. Two
tiles' halves meet exactly at the shared-edge midpoint, so the result is one continuous span that
is identical whichever tile is "from", needs no cross-tile state, and clips cleanly against the
survey fog because a masked neighbour simply draws nothing.

Every one of those properties is wanted here, including the fog behaviour. Adopt the idiom
wholesale; the only differences are which neighbours count (same landform, not same road) and how
the segment is stroked.

**It must not read as a road.** Roads use this exact geometry in warm tan. The ridge needs a
different stroke — serrated/peaked rather than smooth, in `contrast_ink` rather than the road
palette — or the map gains two span families that look alike. This is the main visual risk.

## The three cases

1. **Isolated tile** — no same-landform cardinal neighbour. Keeps BL-231's existing centred glyph.
   Exactly parallel to the road's centre cap, which exists for the same reason.
2. **Run / chain** — one or two same-landform neighbours. Draws the spanning ridge halves. "Wavy"
   is Ben's word and it is the right one: a slight peaked oscillation along the segment reads as
   terrain, where a straight line reads as infrastructure.
3. **Interior** — a tile whose cardinal neighbours are ALL the same landform, i.e. Ben's diamond
   with a filled middle. Draws a filled/hatched interior instead of ridge halves, so a compact
   cluster reads as one massif rather than a knot of crossing lines. The interior tile has no
   exposed edge, which is precisely why the linear treatment fails there.

## Which landforms

**Mountain, rift, canyon** — all three are linear features. Rift is the strongest case of the
three: a fault IS a line, and drawing it as scattered icons is the most wrong of the four.

**Crater stays discrete.** An impact basin is a blob, not a line, and BL-231's flattened-bowl
glyph already says "basin". Spanning craters would produce a shape that means nothing.

## GATE — measure contiguity first, as BL-231 did

BL-231's proportions were decided by a histogram, and that is why its design got simpler instead
of more elaborate. Same discipline here, and the risk is concrete: Pass 5 grows mountain from
seeds where ring 0 is mountain and ring 1 is only 30% mountain, so clusters may be small and
scattered rather than long ranges. If most mountain tiles have no mountain cardinal neighbour,
spanning almost never fires and this is decoration.

So extend `world_audit`'s S3 section with a contiguity readout before building the render:
per linear landform, the share of tiles with 0 / 1 / 2+ same-landform cardinal neighbours, the
share that are interior (all four), and the longest contiguous run. Those three numbers decide
whether case 2 or case 3 is the common one — and whether the item is worth doing at all. Record
them in this item before fixing the visual, exactly as BL-231 recorded its histogram.

## Verification

Extend `scripts/verify/landform_relief.lua` rather than adding a second script — the captures
want to sit beside BL-231's so the before/after is one comparison. Kepler (1.5% mountain, the
sparse case) and Cinder both, since a dry body's larger crater and valley fields exercise the
interior case that Kepler may never produce.

---

## MEASURED 2026-07-31 — the gate ran, and it both confirms and corrects the idea

`world_audit` § S4 (same-landform CARDINAL neighbours, columns wrapping as the canvas does):

| Landform | Tiles | Isolated | End-of-run (1) | In-run (2+) | Interior (4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mountain | 142 | 28.9% | 52.8% | 18.3% | **0.0%** |
| rift | 16 | 18.8% | 56.2% | 25.0% | **0.0%** |
| canyon | 24 | 50.0% | 33.3% | 16.7% | **0.0%** |

**VERDICT: build the span, drop the interior.**

**The span is worth it.** 71% of mountain tiles and 81% of rift tiles have at least one
same-landform neighbour, so the spanning treatment fires on the clear majority of both. The
scattered-specks risk this gate existed to catch did not materialise.

**Run length is ~2-3, exactly as Ben pictured.** With 52.8% of mountain tiles at one neighbour and
18.3% at two or more, most runs are 2 or 3 tiles - a length-3 line contributes two ends and one
middle, which is close to the observed ratio. "Three tiles in a line" was not a hypothetical; it is
the modal shape.

**Case 3 (filled interior) is CANCELLED - it can never fire.** Not one tile in the entire system
has all four cardinal neighbours of the same landform. The diamond-with-a-filled-middle would be
dead code on every seed. This is the measurement paying for itself: the case would have been built,
looked correct in review, and never once appeared on screen.

If a future generation change grows fatter clusters (BL-051's tectonic landforms would), the S4
interior column is already there to show it, and the case can be revived on evidence.

**Canyon is the marginal one.** 50% isolated and only 24 tiles system-wide, so half its glyphs stay
caps and the spanning read is thin. Include it for consistency - the code is shared and excluding it
would be a special case with no benefit - but expect it to carry little.

## Revised scope (supersedes the three cases above)

1. **Isolated** - keeps BL-231's centred glyph. Needed by 29% of mountain, 50% of canyon tiles.
2. **Run** - the spanning ridge halves, BL-172's road-edge idiom. The item's substance.
3. ~~**Interior**~~ - cancelled on measurement, 0.0% across all three landforms.
BL-232.resolution:
LANDED 2026-07-31, scope corrected by its own gate.

THE SPAN. icons::landform_span draws one HALF of a shared edge — tile centre to edge-midpoint — toward each same-landform cardinal neighbour, so the neighbour's half meets it exactly. BL-172's road span/symmetry idiom reused wholesale, including the survey-fog clip (a masked neighbour draws nothing) and the centre-cap role, which the lone tile's centred glyph now plays. Each span echoes its own centred glyph so a run and a lone tile read as one feature: mountain a chain of peaks, rift one continuous fissure, canyon paired rims. Crater never spans.

TWO THINGS THE GEOMETRY HAD TO GET RIGHT. The waveform's perpendicular is CANONICALISED rather than derived from the direction of travel — otherwise the two halves of one span deflect to opposite sides and meet in a kink instead of a wave. And the first mountain profile put two spikes in each half; at four per span the teeth were fine enough that a cluster read as a jagged OUTLINE rather than a ridge, which is precisely what bridging exists to fix. Cut to one peak per half-edge.

THE INTERIOR CASE WAS CANCELLED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY TASTE. world_audit § S4 (added as the gate): 71% of mountain and 81% of rift tiles have a same-landform cardinal neighbour and modal run length is 2-3, so the span fires on the majority. But NOT ONE TILE in the system has all four — the designed filled-interior case would have been dead code on every seed. Found before writing it. S4 also prints exemplar run/lone coordinates, so the verify script points at real runs instead of coordinates eyeballed off a screenshot that silently rot.

THE TOOLTIP (Ben: 'there is no easy way for a player to know what is what'). Every tile hover named the composition and never the landform, in all three variants — so the glyph vocabulary could only be learned by clicking each tile through to the Selection panel, which is not learning. All three now show 'composition · landform', and the plain-canvas variant adds the consequence. Plains stays unnamed: it is the untouched baseline in both channels.

The identical multiplier table is implemented as landform_logistics_cost, a TRAVERSAL cost. BL-231's docs and code comments (and this author's earlier prose) repeated the build-cost claim; all corrected to movement cost, and the discrepancy is recorded in TILES.md as a design call rather than silently rewritten.

The font is loaded with ImGui's DEFAULT glyph range, so the 26 existing '\xe2\x80\x94' em-dashes and '\xe2\x89\xa5' signs across the UI all render as '?' — including bare em-dash placeholders in entity_summary.cpp that therefore read as errors. BL-233.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31 (Ben: "the final step for terrain here, is to add combat modifiers to tiles. This will allow our simulated history to run with a few parameters").

## This is not new scope — it is grading something already load-bearing

`is_barrier` (src/world/history_ladder.cpp:91) already exists and already answers "does this tile
resist an army":

```cpp
if (t.composition == terrain_composition::ocean) return true;
if (t.landform == terrain_landform::mountain)    return true;
if (t.landform == terrain_landform::canyon)      return true;
return t.composition == terrain_composition::barren
    || t.composition == terrain_composition::icy;
```

Its output drives the political map. `barrier_q` feeds `fragmentation_q`, `conquest_cost_q` and
`exit_cost_q`, and `fragmentation_q` feeds `polity_seeds` — the nation count. So terrain combat
value is ALREADY a campaign-shaping parameter; it is simply expressed as one bit per tile.

**Authority already backs the property.** SYSTEMS.md § Environment: "Environment sets the local cost
of construction, **the difficulty of military operations**, and extraction yields." The system is
designed; only its resolution is crude.

**Scope stays clean.** TECH_FOUNDATIONS excludes combat RESOLUTION, opponent AI, unit transport and
weaponry, and this item adds none of them. It also states that units exist in the data model
"defined enough that they will not need to be retrofitted when combat is added" — which is exactly
the standard this item meets. No units, no rules, no AI, no runtime combat.

## The core defect: three different barriers wearing one name

The binary conflates three mechanically distinct things, which is why it cannot be graded in place:

1. **Defensive ground** — mountain, canyon, rift. Hard to attack ACROSS; multiplies a defender.
2. **Attritional ground** — barren, icy, and to a degree regolith. Perfectly crossable, but starves
   an army: no forage, no water, no shelter. It costs the ATTACKER without helping a defender.
3. **Water** — ocean. Not land-crossable at all; a different movement mode, and the thing that makes
   EXIT cheap rather than conquest dear.

HISTORY.md's non-hegemony argument needs these separated, not merged. Its claim is that conquest was
dear WHILE exit was cheap — and `exit_cost_q` already subtracts a coastal term, so the ladder is
already straining against the single boolean it is given.

## The design

Two pure functions in a new `src/world/terrain_combat.{hpp,cpp}`, parallel in shape and spirit to
`landform_logistics_cost` — no stored field, no component change, **no serialisation seam**, and
deterministic by construction:

- **`terrain_defence(composition, landform)`** — how well the ground holds against an attacker.
  Landform dominates (mountain highest, then rift/canyon, then highland; plains/valley near zero),
  with composition modulating (forest and wetland conceal and impede; grassland is open ground).
- **`terrain_attrition(composition, landform)`** — what crossing costs an army in supply,
  independent of any defender. Driven by composition (barren, icy, regolith high; grassland and
  wetland low) and mildly by landform.

Water stays its own explicit test rather than becoming a third scalar, because it is a **mode**
change, not a magnitude — the same reason logistics already branches land/sea.

**`is_barrier` is then deleted**, and `barrier_q` is recomputed from the graded fields. Keeping
both would leave two sources of truth for the same question, which is how the current drift started.

## THE RISK, stated plainly

Grading the barrier field **will move the nation count**. `barrier_q` is a share of tiles today;
graded, it becomes a mean intensity, and `fragmentation_q` -> `polity_seeds` moves with it. Ben
personally set that number when BL-221 landed (14 -> 43, an explicitly measured decision).

So the same discipline applies and is **not optional here**: implement the scalars, measure
fragmentation / conquest / exit / polity_seeds and the resulting nation count against the current
values, and **put both sets of numbers to Ben before any constant is locked**. Do not tune to
preserve today's 43 — that would be fitting the model to an outcome, which is the opposite of the
"driven, not narrated" rule this whole ladder was built under. If the honest graded field says a
different number, that is the finding.

## What it unlocks

**BL-224's non-hegemony assertions become assertable.** N4 ("terrain barriers actually land on
borders at better than chance") and N5 ("the largest nation cannot cheaply reach the smallest —
conquest cost above a floor") both read terrain conquest cost. Against a boolean, N4 can only ask
whether borders touch mountains; against a graded field it can ask whether borders sit on
DEFENSIBLE ground, which is the actual claim.

**BL-239 (culture regions) gets a better clustering field** — its comment already notes it will
cluster on "the SAME barriers" this function computes.

## Verification

- `history_ladder_harness`: the graded field is deterministic; monotonicity (a strictly more
  defensible world never scores lower fragmentation); both extremes stay inside their clamps.
- `world_audit`: report mean/max defence and attrition per body alongside the S3/S4 landform
  sections, so a tuning change that flattens the field is visible — the same guard S3 gives.
- The before/after political-map numbers above, recorded in this item.

## Explicitly NOT in this item

Runtime combat, units, unit stats, sieges, fortification buildings, or any AI use of these values.
The functions are consumed at generation time only. A later combat layer reads the same two
functions, which is the point of writing them as the authority now.
BL-233.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. is_barrier is deleted; the history ladder now prices conquest from the graded field.

THE ADOPTED FORMULA. barrier_q = mean(terrain_resistance) over LAND tiles + ocean_share * k_ocean_barrier_weight/1000, with the weight at 750. Water is its own term rather than folded into the terrain signal -- Ben's call 2026-07-31, taken over both alternatives (water at zero, water at full weight).

THE WEIGHT WAS CHOSEN BY SWEEP, NOT BY TASTE. Kepler nation count across the knob, against a committed binary baseline of 30 nations / 37 realms: w=0 -> 17/23, w=250 -> 17/23, w=500 -> 17/26, w=750 -> 30/33, w=1000 -> 36/50. 750 holds the political map Ben set while the land term still does its job. That this is a deliberate choice of continuity -- not a number that fell out -- is recorded in the constant's own doc comment so a later re-tune knows.

THE DEFECTS ARE FIXED. Pallas's barrier field was a flat ZERO (no mountain or canyon, compositions outside the barren/icy pair, so a high-attrition metallic body read as open ground) and is now 325. Per-body land means now separate where the boolean gave one bit: defence 80/88/130/135, attrition 509/694/696/777. Kepler's field barely moves (732 -> 722) because its 588 ocean tiles keep most of their weight, which is exactly what choosing 750 bought.

world_audit S5 was rewritten from a measurement-only comparison into the standing report of the adopted field, keeping the retired binary as the fixed reference point and the defence/attrition means as the tuning guard the design asked for.

Verified: history_ladder_harness ALL PASS, world_audit PASS, determinism_harness + world_determinism PASS, 33/34 ctest (the one failure is BL-252, pre-existing and unrelated). No stored field, no component change, nothing on the serialisation seam. Still no combat resolution, units or AI.

BL-234.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31, found while building BL-232's landform tooltip.

## The defect

`src/ui/fonts.cpp:46` calls `AddFontFromFileTTF(path, size_px, &cfg)` with **no `GlyphRanges`**,
so ImGui builds its default atlas — Basic Latin + Latin-1 Supplement, U+0020..U+00FF. Any codepoint
above that renders as the not-found glyph, "?".

26 UI strings are above it. Two characters account for all of them: **em-dash U+2014**
(`"\xe2\x80\x94"`) and **greater-than-or-equal U+2265** (`"\xe2\x89\xa5"`).

The bundled **DejaVuSans has both glyphs** — nothing is missing from the font. Only the requested
range is too narrow.

## Why it is worse than cosmetic

Several sites are a **bare** em-dash used as a placeholder — `entity_summary.cpp` lines 100, 128,
162, 195, all `ImGui::TextDisabled("\xe2\x80\x94")` with the comment "em-dash: stale/missing
selection". Those cells currently draw a lone **"?"**, which does not read as "nothing selected" —
it reads as *the app does not know*, i.e. as an error state. The intended meaning is inverted.

The BL-069 workforce tooltip's "habitability \u2265 0.6" likewise loses its operator, leaving
"habitability ? 0.6".

## The fix

Pass an explicit glyph range to `AddFontFromFileTTF`. Either `GetGlyphRangesDefault()` extended
with the two blocks actually used (General Punctuation U+2000..U+206F for the dashes and quotes, and
the handful of Mathematical Operators around U+2265), or a static `ImWchar` range built to cover
exactly the characters the UI ships. Prefer the narrow explicit range: it keeps the atlas small and
makes the supported set legible in one place, so the next person adding a "·" or a "→" can see
whether it is covered.

**The range must live beside the font load, with a comment naming the constraint** — otherwise the
next UI string above U+00FF reintroduces the bug silently, which is exactly what happened here.

## Verification

Visual. Capture a frame containing a bare-em-dash placeholder (an empty Selection panel) and the
BL-069 population tooltip, and confirm the dash and the \u2265 draw as themselves. Worth a blessed
golden, since the failure mode is silent and a future font change could reintroduce it.

## Note

BL-232's landform tooltip deliberately stays inside Latin-1 ("Convoys pay ×N to cross", using
U+00D7) so it renders correctly today. Once this lands, that constraint can be relaxed, but the
string is fine as-is and needs no revisit.
BL-234.resolution:

BL-247.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31 (Ben, same session as the BL-214 fold-model revision — see that item's supersession note).

## What this is, precisely

A small, closed-by-default affordance attached to every chart/visual: a toggle reading 'Why this chart', which reveals exactly two lines:

- **Answers:** <the question this specific chart, here, answers> — phrased as a real question a player would ask, not a chart caption.
- **Because:** <why this particular evidence justifies that answer> — one sentence, plain, no hedging.

It is co-located with the chart it describes (not a separate panel, not a global FAQ), closed by default (so the folded/narrow reading this whole design arc has been chasing stays narrow), and revealed by an explicit click — never shown automatically, never animated into view unprompted.

## What this explicitly is NOT (the correction)

Ben's original phrase 'asking interesting questions' was read, in the first pass of this design session, as a Q&A-driven navigation model — a list of pre-written questions ('Why is my Iron Ore extractor losing money?') that the game answers on the player's behalf when clicked (prototyped as build_UI_example_4). Ben corrected this directly: a tutorial, or any in-game help surface, must never tell the player what they should be asking or answering — only how to navigate the information that is already there. build_UI_example_4's Q&A list is therefore NOT carried into implementation as the drill-through mechanism; it remains on disk as a discarded exploration, not a reference design. The chart question log is a different, narrower thing: it documents what a chart that already exists is FOR, after the fact, on request - it does not curate a path through the game or pre-digest which questions matter.

## The dual audience

1. **Player-facing**, lightly: a player who wonders why a particular chart is even here can find out without it being forced on them, and without the game pretending to know what THEY specifically want to ask next.
2. **Design-facing, for Ben**: authoring the Answers/Because pair for a new chart is itself a check - a chart that cannot state a real question and a real justification in one sentence each probably does not earn its place. Reading the log across an existing view is also how Ben means to navigate the UI himself when looking for the next interesting question to add, or when deciding a candidate question is too large to answer in a single visual and needs to be split or deferred.

## Relationship to BL-214's Study-tier derivation captions

This is a distinct axis from BL-214's (now-superseded, but conceptually still relevant) derivation captions and threshold labels. A derivation caption answers 'how was this number computed' (e.g. 'base 23.6/tick × 0.78 hazard factor'). The chart question log answers 'why does this chart exist at all, and what is it for' (e.g. 'is this tile worth extracting Iron Ore from, compared to the best tiles I've surveyed'). A chart can have one without the other, but most will want both — the derivation is evidence, the question/justification is intent. Implementers should not conflate the two into one blob of text; they answer different questions and a reader may want one without the other.

## Reference implementation

build_UI_example_1/index.html and build_UI_example_2/index.html both carry a working preview: a small '? Why this chart' toggle beside each chart's legend, a closed-by-default note with the additive-reveal CSS pattern (grid-template-rows 0fr -> 1fr) already used elsewhere in this design arc, and per-chart question/why strings authored alongside the chart's own data. In the History Ledger exemplar every chart across all five stages carries its own pair, demonstrating that the pattern scales per-chart rather than per-panel.

## Open for the promoting session

1. Whether every chart is required to carry a question/why pair, or whether it is optional and a missing one simply shows no toggle (the exemplars always populate it; a real audit pass would need to decide whether an unlabelled chart is a defect or an acceptable gap).
2. Whether the toggle's open/closed state persists per-session like BL-214's old detail level did, or always resets closed on each view open (the exemplars always reset closed - the note is meant to be read once, not to become a way of reading the chart's normal content).
3. Whether this belongs as a per-chart parameter on the shared chart-drawing helpers in charts.cpp / generation_charts.cpp (recommended - it should be as cheap to add as passing two more strings) or a separate wrapper call site.
BL-247.resolution: Complete. ui::why_note - a closed-by-default "? Why this chart" toggle revealing exactly two lines (Answers:/Because:) and nothing more. Its three open questions are settled: (1) the pair is OPTIONAL, a chart with no authored pair draws no toggle, since forcing one would manufacture prose and a missing pair is a review signal not a render defect; (2) one note open at a time, reset closed by any expand/fold; (3) it is a per-chart parameter on the shared chart_row helper, so authoring one costs two strings beside the data it describes. Lives in detail_level.{hpp,cpp} rather than charts.cpp as filed - it needs ui_state, and charts:: is deliberately a pure draw-primitive namespace. Pairs authored for all 14 generation charts, the Selection band s metric chart, and the four corp roll-ups. The chart row RESERVES the note s measured height before opening its fixed-size child, so an open note cannot clip - this item does not create the fitting defect BL-215 is queued to audit. 4 goldens blessed.

BL-248.design:
DESIGNED 2026-07-31 (Ben, same session as BL-214/BL-247), reference implementation build_UI_example_3/index.html (rebuilt once after an accidental mid-session tree wipe; NOTES.md in that folder records the rebuild and its own judgment calls).

## What this item is

Promote MENU.md's Slot 1 (Corporation overview dashboard, design settled 2026-06-15, [B3]) from named-but-unbuilt to an actual buildable item, using the interaction mechanics this session settled: every roll-up card folds to one line by default (BL-214's binary fold model - no in-place growth, a real full-screen mode-switch on demand), each roll-up's chart(s) carry a closed-by-default 'why this chart' log (BL-247), and clicking into a roll-up's specific chart element (a bar, a line point) opens a narrower BL-196 child drill scoped to just that one subject, breadcrumbed back to the roll-up.

## The roll-up-set decision (settled 2026-07-31)

MENU.md's original MVP set (§ Slot 1) was: **balance + last-tick delta**, a **holdings roll-up** (building count / bodies present), **workforce contention**, and **alerts** (idle buildings, unsold output, negative cashflow) - each line clicking through into the relevant per-system ledger (a HOST-axis navigation, not a Depth/Subject drill). build_UI_example_3 instead built four roll-ups titled **Production, Trade, Workforce, Finance**, each foldable to full-screen with its own per-item drill and chart question log.

These were not the same four things, and this item originally left the choice open. Ben resolved it directly (2026-07-31, asked explicitly rather than assumed): **the exemplar's four roll-ups (Production/Trade/Workforce/Finance) supersede MENU.md's MVP set.** This IS the 'fuller dashboard design pass' MENU.md flags as owed for v0.1.1 - not a competing alternative to it. Landing this item therefore includes updating MENU.md's § Slot 1 text to describe Production/Trade/Workforce/Finance (with their fold/drill/why-log behaviour) in place of the old Balance/Holdings/Contention/Alerts MVP description; the authority doc is intentionally left unchanged until then, per the standing 'authority doc updates when the work lands' rule. MENU.md's per-line click-through-to-ledger idea is not lost - it survives as the HOST axis (`[>]`), available alongside the drill rather than instead of it, exactly as this item's 'What ships either way' section already described.

## What ships either way

Regardless of which roll-up-set question resolves which way, the following is common:

- Four cards in a 2x2 grid (or whatever grid the chosen roll-up count needs), each independently foldable per BL-214's binary model - one verdict line by default, a chevron to a true full-screen overlay, never an in-place grow.
- Each full-screen roll-up's chart(s) carry BL-247's chart question log.
- Per-card drills into narrower, roll-up-specific subjects (a building, a route, a ledger line) with a breadcrumb + back control, per BL-196 - build_UI_example_3 demonstrates four genuinely different drill shapes rather than one shared generic detail panel, which is the property to preserve regardless of which four roll-ups are chosen.
- If MENU.md's click-through-to-ledger behaviour is kept (option b above), that is the HOST axis (`[>]`/`focus_on_entity`), layered alongside rather than instead of the drill - the two are orthogonal per BL-214's three-axis model, not competing.

## Reference implementation

build_UI_example_3/index.html - a self-contained HTML/CSS/JS mock, live-interactive, verified this session (fold/expand on all four cards, four distinct drills, chart question logs, and a scenario switch that re-keys every card's figures live without disturbing per-card fold or drill state). Its NOTES.md documents the mock's own judgment calls (e.g. folding a card also closes any open drill within it; only Finance's headline is clickable since its drill isn't per-item). Treat the INTERACTION code (the fold/drill/why-log wiring, reusable from BL-214/BL-247's own landed implementations) as the transferable part; treat the specific mock numbers, building names, and roll-up choice as illustrative, not sourced from real game data.

## Open for the promoting session

1. Whether the dashboard opens as the shell-column fold-out MENU.md now describes (2026-07-31 note, superseding the original floating-window design) or some other placement - MENU.md is authoritative here, this item does not revisit shell placement.
2. Real data wiring: which world/economy_system fields actually populate Production/Trade/Workforce/Finance - not designed here, this item is the surface and interaction, not the economy-side plumbing. (Note this is now the settled roll-up set, not the MENU.md MVP fields.)
BL-248.resolution: Complete. Nav slot 1 is now the real dashboard: Production / Trade / Workforce / Finance as four roll-up cards, each resting as ONE verdict line and expanding through BL-214 s shared chevron to a full-screen view with its chart, that chart s question log, and a per-item drill breadcrumbed back to the roll-up. The four drills are four DIFFERENT shapes - a building s operating economics (through the shared draw_building_profit builder, now declared in the header rather than being an undeclared file-local definition), a lane s completed convoys and recency, a building s assigned-against-effective labour, and the budget s five flows for Finance, whose subject is not per-item. Every figure is derived from the live world + economy_report; the exemplar s scenario numbers were not carried over. The old all-corporations balance table was RETIRED (corporation_panel.{hpp,cpp} deleted) - it was a cross-corp comparison surface, not the player corp at a glance, and duplicated the Economy panel s Corps view. MENU.md Slot 1 rewritten. Known honest gap: the generated world seeds every market on one body, so the Trade card reads 0 lanes until that is settled (the open design question BL-254 deliberately left). 9 goldens blessed.

BL-249.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 1 into a buildable item.

## Why it needed filing

The three audit instruments are a **cut gate** — ROADMAP § v0.1.0 lists them between the terrain
strand and "the Cut" — but none of the three existed as a backlog item, so nothing owned them and
the done-definition could not be checked off. This files the first.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Frame budget. Frame-time HUD: last / avg / max ms + 1% lows. Targets: avg < 8 ms, max < 16.7 ms
panning the full Kepler tile grid (15,120 tiles). If max spikes the HUD says why — GPU present,
draw-call volume, or allocation churn."

## Shape

A self-contained `src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp}`: a ring buffer of recent frame times plus the
derived last / avg / max / 1%-low, and the HUD draw. Wired from the `app.cpp` frame loop, which
carries NO frame instrumentation today (one `SDL_GetTicks` call at app.cpp:3136, unrelated).

**Off by default and toggleable** — it is an audit instrument, not shipped chrome — and therefore
subject to the standing toggle rule (clicking an active control undoes it).

## The honesty constraint on "says why"

The ROADMAP names three spike causes: GPU present, draw-call volume, allocation churn. Only report
the ones actually measurable from inside the frame loop — time in the render/present call, and
ImGui's own draw-list vertex/command counts. **Do not fabricate an allocation-churn figure that is
not really being measured**; an instrument that invents its own numbers is worse than no
instrument, because the audit then rests on it. If a named cause cannot be measured, the item
records that rather than papering over it.

## Not in scope

Optimisation. This measures; acting on what it finds is separate work.
BL-249.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp} plus F11, off by default.

Reports last / avg / max / 1% low against the ROADMAP targets (avg < 8 ms, max < 16.7 ms), colouring a breached figure. On a spike it breaks the worst frame down into build / submit / present / other, with ImGui's own vertex and draw-command counts.

HONEST ABOUT ITS LIMITS, which was the constraint set on it: the ROADMAP named "allocation churn" as a spike cause, and the HUD prints "allocation churn: not instrumented" rather than inventing a figure. The other/build/submit/present split is real, and on the verification capture it correctly attributed a 196 ms frame to "event pump + simulation step" (other 185.78 ms) rather than to rendering — the instrument diagnosing correctly on its first real spike.

OFF BY DEFAULT and verified so: scripts/verify/frame_budget_hud.lua capture 1 is an ordinary frame with no HUD present, which is what keeps every other golden in the suite unaffected by this instrument existing. Toggle rule honoured — F11 while open puts it away.

Drawn on both frame paths (the pre-play early-return branch and in-game), which are mutually exclusive, so it is not double-drawn.

INTEGRATION WIRING added in the main session: the show_panel("frame_hud", open) verify binding the slice assumed but did not add, without which the HUD could not be captured at all.

The absolute frame numbers under --verify are meaningless (offscreen driver, no vsync, no real present) and the verify script says so in its header. The 8 ms / 16.7 ms targets remain a human-in-the-loop measurement against the real app panning the full Kepler grid.

BL-250.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 2 into a buildable item.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Econ-tick scaling. Extend `econ_stability` to print tick time. Target: well under 1 ms for the
prototype world; confirm it does not grow faster than linearly in bodies x corps."

## Shape

Extends the EXISTING `tools/verify/econ_stability.cpp` rather than adding a harness — the loop it
already drives (run_economy_step -> clear_markets -> apply_budget over 100 ticks) is exactly the
thing being timed, and a second harness would duplicate its world setup.

Three additions: per-tick wall clock reported as mean / max / p95; a sweep across several
bodies x corps sizes with the growth ratio between successive sizes; and an assertion that the
prototype-scale tick sits well under 1 ms.

## The flakiness constraint

An absolute-time assertion on a shared or loaded machine is a false-failure generator. So the
**shape** is the real check — the growth ratio, which is machine-independent — and the absolute
bound is set generously enough to catch an order-of-magnitude regression without tripping on a
busy CI box. The harness states its own tolerance in its output rather than hiding it in a
constant.

Timing must be strictly additive: every existing assertion and every line of existing output
survives unchanged. Measurement must never become a behaviour change.
BL-250.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. tools/verify/econ_stability.cpp gained per-tick timing and a bodies x corps scaling sweep; every pre-existing assertion (R1-R4) survives unchanged.

Prototype scale: mean 0.0018 ms, p95 0.0021 ms, max 0.0409 ms per tick — 555x headroom against the 1 ms ROADMAP target.

The sweep runs six rungs from 1 body / 8 corps to 8 bodies / 256 corps and reads growth off the MIN per-tick time, not the mean: preemption can only ever ADD time, so the fastest tick is the cleanest estimate of true cost and the ladder's shape survives a loaded machine. That design choice is what makes the check non-flaky, which was the binding constraint.

Result: 32x size -> 83.1x time, i.e. time ~ size^1.28, against a tolerance of size^1.5 (linear 1.0, quadratic 2.0). The largest swept world, 128x prototype, still ticks under 1 ms.

IT FOUND SOMETHING, which is the point of an instrument. The exponent sits above 1.0 because run_corp_strategic_step rescans every tile for every due corp — an O(corps x tiles) term, a rounding error to ~64 corps and about half the tick by 256. Filed as BL-253 rather than fixed here; the sweep now asserts the exponent stays under 1.5, so a regression trips a test.

BL-251.design:
FILED 2026-07-31. Promotes ROADMAP § v0.1.0 "Audit instruments" bullet 3 into a buildable item.

## The spec (verbatim from ROADMAP)

"Data creep. Entity/pool/market/convoy counters + RSS memory readout run long (100 -> 1000+ ticks):
counts and memory must plateau, not climb. A steady climb on an idle run names the unbounded
structure."

## Shape

A NEW `tools/verify/data_creep_harness.cpp` over the REAL generated world
(`make_hard_coded_world()`), not a toy — an unbounded structure is a property of the real data
model, and a hand-built world would not exhibit it. Samples at 100 / 250 / 500 / 1000+ ticks:
entity count, every component-store size, pool count, market and order-book sizes, convoy count,
trade-route count, and RSS (via /proc/self/statm, guarded so a non-Linux build still compiles and
reports RSS unavailable).

"Plateau" is defined numerically in the harness output — the 1000-tick value within a stated
tolerance of the 500-tick value — rather than left to the reader.

## The point is the NAMING

A bare "something grew" is not actionable. When a counter climbs the harness must say WHICH
store/collection and by how much; that is the whole instrument, and the reason it is worth more
than eyeballing RSS.

## Expected to find something

This is the first instrument ever pointed at data growth, so a genuine unbounded structure is a
plausible outcome. If one is found: **report it, do not weaken the assertion to go green, and do
not fix the growth inside this item** — the instrument's job is to name it. The fix is separate,
itemised work, sized once the finding is real.
BL-251.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-07-31. tools/verify/data_creep_harness.cpp runs the REAL generated world (make_hard_coded_world) for 1500 ticks, sampling ~30 counters plus process RSS at five marks, and asserts each plateaus between the mid and final sample.

Result: every exercised counter is flat from tick 500 to 1500 — entities 34769, tiles 34440, buildings/stockpiles 259, markets 6, nations 30, pools 8, tile_to_nation 6216 — and RSS plateaus at 13980 KiB. No unbounded structure among them. Runtime 7.4 s (world gen 0.15 s + 1500 ticks at 4.8 ms/tick).

IT REPORTED ITS OWN BLIND SPOT rather than passing quietly, which is the behaviour worth preserving: no convoy was dispatched anywhere in the run, so world.convoys, world.trade_routes and world.body_last_glimpse_tick sat at 0 throughout and their plateau assertions passed VACUOUSLY. The harness says so explicitly in a COVERAGE section, and names world.trade_routes as never-erased by construction — the very shape the instrument exists to catch. Filed as BL-254.

world.ai_decisions is a fixed 256-entry ring (constant across all samples); its running total climbing 270 -> 2277 is reported as informational, not asserted, which is correct.

BL-252.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31, on the first run of the whole suite on Linux/GCC (the cloud session that
closed the v0.1.0 cut set). Filed rather than fixed — the fix is a policy call, not a code change.

## The observation, stated precisely

**Headless.** `ai_skill_harness` fails 8 golden-band assertions. Critically, its own determinism
tier passes completely:

- R0: state_hash identical at every sampled tick across two same-seed runs — PASS
- R0: net-worth curve byte-identical across two same-seed runs — PASS
- R0: action-verb tallies identical — PASS

So determinism WITHIN this platform is intact. What differs is the value against bands blessed on
Windows/MSVC. Seed 0 passes; seeds 1-4 drift, some well outside the band (seed 1 final net worth
211,116 against a band of 250,000-560,000).

**Visual.** Every `--verify` script diffs against its golden: 9.5% on hover_freeze, 21.6% on
building_management_panel, 43-57% on the selection/visibility captures. Font rasterisation alone
would explain a few percent; these are larger.

## The two candidate causes — NOT yet distinguished

1. **Cross-platform float divergence, amplified.** 300 ticks of a feedback-coupled economy is a
   chaotic system; a last-bit difference in one price compounds. This would explain why seed 0
   survives and others do not — divergence is seed-dependent, not uniform.
2. **Stale goldens.** The bands were blessed 2026-07-31 from "a first pass of this exact harness";
   if anything landed after that pass, they are simply out of date.

Distinguishing them is cheap and is the item's first task: re-run the harness on Windows at the
same commit. Identical-to-band means platform; drifted-there-too means stale. **Do not re-bless
before knowing which** — re-blessing a platform divergence would just move the redness to the
other machine.

## Why it matters now, not later

The v0.1.0 done-definition requires "headless harnesses green". With platform-dependent goldens
that phrase has no single truth value, and the quality audit (BL-249/250/251) is measured on
whichever machine happens to run it. This is a cut blocker in effect, which is why it is rated A.

## The policy question to settle

Whether goldens are (a) platform-pinned — one blessed set per toolchain, selected at runtime;
(b) widened until platform-independent, accepting weaker regression detection; or (c) declared
Windows-authoritative, with the Linux suite running only the platform-independent tiers (R0
determinism, the structural harnesses) — which is what actually holds today, undocumented.

The visual goldens likely answer differently from the headless bands: pixel output depends on
font rasterisation and GPU/driver, so (c) may be right for visual while (a) or (b) fits headless.

## Not in scope

Making the numbers match across platforms. Bit-identical floating point across MSVC and GCC is not
a goal this prototype should adopt — the standing determinism invariant is same-seed, same-build
reproducibility, which is intact.
BL-252.resolution:
COMPLETE 2026-08-01. The item asked for a diagnostic first and a policy call second; both were done, and the diagnostic changed the answer.

DIAGNOSTIC — the two candidate causes are BOTH real and independent, not one or the other.
  (1) STALE. Re-running the harness on Windows/MSVC at the same commit FAILED 5 assertions — on the very platform the bands were blessed on. The bands were authored from the first run of the harness, in the commit that ADDED it (8542e4b); BL-203 (Corp AI stage B: strategy layer, priority buckets, predictive spending), BL-221 (pre-national ladder) and BL-233 (terrain combat modifiers) all landed afterwards. The AI was substantially rewritten after its own goldens were set, and BL-221/BL-233 reshape the political map every seed generates. So the Windows drift was fully EXPLAINED, and re-blessing there was the sanctioned action, not a judgement call.
  (2) PLATFORM. Cross-platform divergence is also real and large. Same commit, Linux/GCC -O2 vs Windows/MSVC: seed 0 final 395143.0 vs 206245.2, seed 4 182745.5 vs 392148.4 — up to ~2x. Each platform is perfectly deterministic within itself (R0 passes on both).
  CONFOUND REMOVED: optimisation level is NOT the variable. MSVC /O2 reproduces MSVC Debug value for value, byte for byte. The toolchain is.

POLICY — settled by Ben 2026-08-01, and the two golden families answer DIFFERENTLY.
  Headless bands: PINNED PER TOOLCHAIN. ai_skill_harness now carries one blessed set per compiler behind #if defined(_MSC_VER) / #elif defined(__GNUC__), with an #error for any third toolchain so it cannot silently inherit another set. Both platforms now report ALL PASS (0 failures). Option (b) — widen until platform-independent — was measured and REJECTED, not assumed: a band holding both platforms would span roughly +/-100% and would detect no plausible regression.
  Visual goldens: WINDOWS-AUTHORITATIVE. Blessed and diffed on Windows only; on Linux, captures are inspected by eye and not golden-diffed. Pixel output depends on font rasterisation and GPU/driver as well as the toolchain, so a per-platform pin would mean re-blessing on every driver update for no detection gain.

NOT A DETERMINISM FAILURE. The standing invariant is same-seed, same-BUILD reproducibility, and it holds on each platform independently — R0 (state hash, net-worth curve, action tallies byte-identical across two same-seed runs) passes on both. Bit-identical FP across MSVC and GCC remains explicitly out of scope, as the item said.

Policy recorded in docs/development/DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md (new section: Cross-platform goldens), including the re-blessing rule (change only the set for the platform you ran on) and the corollary that a long-unblessed band reading red is usually staleness, not regression.

THE OWED RE-BLESS IS DONE (2026-08-01, same session). The four tile_build_ledger goldens were inspected, then re-blessed on Windows; all now pass at 0.0000%. Worth recording what the inspection found, because it changes what the number meant: tile_build_ledger_land_select — which has NO ledger open — diffed 21.69%, against 22.04% for the capture that does. So only ~0.35% of that diff was BL-162 row anatomy; ~21.7% was whole-canvas world-generation drift from BL-221/BL-233, the same drift that staled the ai_skill bands. BL-254.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31, self-reported by the BL-251 harness in its COVERAGE section:

    NOTE: no convoy was dispatched anywhere in this run, so the convoy /
          trade-route / glimpse-stamp plateaus above are VACUOUS — those
          structures were never exercised. `world.trade_routes` in
          particular is documented as never-erased (components.hpp §
          trade_route), i.e. accumulating by construction; this rollout
          does not bound it. A convoy-exercising scenario is owed.

## Why this matters more than the other counters

Everything the harness DOES exercise plateaus cleanly — entities, tiles, buildings,
stockpiles, markets, nations, pools, RSS, all flat from tick 500 to 1500. The three
structures it does not exercise are the three with the most reason to grow:

- **`world.trade_routes`** is documented as never erased. A route is upserted on convoy
  completion and never removed, so it accumulates monotonically in the number of distinct
  body-pairs traded. Bounded by pairs (small) rather than by ticks — probably fine, but
  "probably fine by argument" is exactly what an instrument is supposed to replace.
- **`world.convoys`** should drain as convoys arrive; a leak here is a live-object leak.
- **`world.body_last_glimpse_tick`** gains an entry per glimpsed body.

## The work

Drive convoy traffic in the rollout so all three are non-zero and repeatedly cycled — the
harness already has `seed_convoy`-style helpers available in the supply layer (see
scripts/verify/proximity_glimpse.lua and tools/verify/trade_routes_harness.cpp for how
existing checks manufacture convoy activity). Then let the plateau assertions bind, and
report what they find.

Rated v0.1.0 because it closes a hole in a v0.1.0 cut gate: the data-creep instrument is
one of the three audit instruments, and it currently cannot see the structure most likely
to creep.

## Credit where due

The harness FOUND AND REPORTED THIS ITSELF rather than passing quietly. That is the
behaviour to preserve in any future instrument — a vacuous pass reported as vacuous is
worth more than a green tick.

BL-255.design:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by the verifier-review barrier over the v0.1.0 audit batch.

## Two coupled hazards

**1. No default build type.** CMakeLists.txt never sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. For a multi-config generator (MSVC) that is fine - check.bat passes --config Release. For a single-config generator (Ninja, Unix Makefiles - i.e. every Linux and cloud session) an unspecified build type means NO optimisation flags at all, and --config is silently ignored.

That matters now in a way it did not before, because BL-250 added assertions with real margins:
  - largest swept rung 0.2932 ms against a 1 ms bound (3.4x headroom)
  - growth exponent 1.28 against a 1.5 tolerance
  - worst single doubling 3.17x against a 4.0x ceiling

A -O0 build is routinely 5-10x slower. The 1 ms bound would fail, and the exponent could shift, for reasons that have nothing to do with the economy loop.

Fix: set a default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (Release, or RelWithDebInfo) when the generator is single-config and the user has not chosen one. Standard three-line idiom.

**2. No test timeouts.** No set_tests_properties(... TIMEOUT ...) exists anywhere. The suite now contains two genuinely long tests (data_creep_harness ~7 s, econ_stability's sweep, corp_terrain_matrix ~9 s). A harness that hangs - an infinite loop in a future economy change is exactly the class - blocks CI on the default 1500 s ctest timeout rather than failing fast.

## Not urgent, but cheap

Neither has bitten yet: the Linux build in the session that found this was configured with an explicit -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, which is why the numbers came out clean. It is filed so the next person configuring without that flag gets a comprehensible failure instead of a mysterious one.
BL-255.completion_note: COMPLETE 2026-08-01. CMakeLists.txt now sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release via the standard GENERATOR_IS_MULTI_CONFIG guard, CACHE STRING, only when the generator is single-config and unset - MSVC/multi-config (check.bat's --config Release) untouched, and an explicit user choice (including Debug) is never overridden. Every ctest test now carries a TIMEOUT: 60s default, 120s for the three named structurally-long harnesses (corp_terrain_matrix, econ_stability, data_creep_harness), applied uniformly in the tools/verify/*.cpp glob loop that registers every add_test call. Verified on WSL2/Ubuntu+Ninja (the single-config case this item is about; MSVC was never affected). Real measurements: default-configure resolved to Release automatically (confirmed via CMakeCache.txt); an explicit -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug configure was preserved unchanged; 33/33 tests carry a TIMEOUT; the suite ran clean at 32/33 pass on both a Release and a from-scratch Debug build (only ai_skill_harness fails, on golden bands - BL-252, pre-existing, out of scope). Slowest Debug/-O0 runtimes measured: corp_terrain_matrix 20.16s (its 120s TIMEOUT is the tightest margin at ~6x), ai_skill_harness 11.00s, history_ladder_harness 8.18s, planetology_harness 7.45s, road_generation_harness 5.80s - all comfortably inside their tier. STALE-BASE GAP, RECONCILED ON MERGE 2026-08-01: the agent worktree was cut from a base predating BL-250 s econ_stability timing sweep and containing neither data_creep_harness.cpp nor font_glyph_harness.cpp, so it could not build or measure them and said so. The integrated tree has all three. Verified post-merge: tools/verify/ contains corp_terrain_matrix.cpp, econ_stability.cpp (with the BL-250 sweep), data_creep_harness.cpp and font_glyph_harness.cpp, and the tools/verify/*.cpp glob loop assigns each a TIMEOUT, so the three named long-runners inherit the 120s tier as intended. Their runtimes under the integrated tree have not been re-measured against those bounds; the integrating ctest run covers that.

BL-258.design:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by the integrating ctest run of the v0.1.0 cut set, on Windows.

## The observation

`econ_stability` fails exactly one assertion on the Windows `build/` tree:

    FAIL  R6 the largest swept world (8 bodies, 256 corps, 128x prototype) still ticks under 1 ms

Everything around it passes, which is what makes the diagnosis clean:

- R5 (prototype-scale tick under 1 ms) PASSES, with **19x headroom** — mean 0.0524 ms.
- R6 growth exponent PASSES (no worse than size^1.5).
- R6 no-single-doubling-costs-4x PASSES.
- R6 finiteness PASSES.
- The same assertion PASSES on Linux/GCC in a Release build (35/35 green).

So the SHAPE assertions — the ones that would catch a real algorithmic regression — all hold. The only failure is the single ABSOLUTE wall-clock bound, at the largest swept rung.

## The cause, and why BL-255 did not close it

The Windows `build/` tree is configured `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` — deliberately, since it is the tree used for debugging the app. A -O0 build is routinely 5-10x slower, which is the whole reason BL-250's absolute bound cannot hold there.

BL-255 fixed the adjacent hazard: a single-config generator with NO build type specified now defaults to Release. It cannot help here, because Debug is not unset — it is chosen. The two are different failure modes and BL-255 correctly did not claim this one.

## Why this matters

"Headless harnesses green" is part of the v0.1.0 done-definition. Today that phrase is false on the Windows tree a developer actually works in, for a reason that has nothing to do with the economy loop. That is the same class of problem BL-252 just fixed for the goldens: an assertion whose truth depends on how the tree happens to be configured teaches the reader to ignore a red result, which is exactly how a real regression gets waved through.

## The fix — gate the absolute bound, keep the shape assertions

The absolute-time assertion is only meaningful against an optimised build. It should either:

1. **Skip with a loud, explicit message** when the build is unoptimised (`#ifndef NDEBUG`, or read the configured build type), printing something like `SKIP R6 absolute tick bound - unoptimised build, timing is not meaningful` rather than silently passing; or
2. **Assert a Debug-specific, generously-scaled bound**, if a number can be defended.

Option 1 is preferred and matches the project's existing standard for this exact situation: the data-creep instrument (BL-251/BL-254) reports a vacuous check AS vacuous rather than as a pass. A skipped-and-said-so check is worth more than a green tick, and far more than a red one everybody learns to ignore.

**Do not simply widen the 1 ms bound to accommodate Debug.** That would destroy its value in Release, where it is the number the ROADMAP actually cares about. The growth-shape assertions must keep running in both configurations — they are dimensionless and hold regardless of optimisation.

## Not in scope

Changing the Windows tree to Release, or the economy loop's performance. The measured Release numbers are healthy (0.0018 ms/tick at prototype scale, 555x headroom) and `run_corp_strategic_step`'s O(corps x tiles) scan is already filed separately as BL-253.
BL-258.resolution: Gated R6 absolute tick bound (Windows Debug tree) behind #ifndef NDEBUG — skips with a loud SKIP line citing BL-258 rather than failing red or silently passing. Release/optimised builds still assert the real 1ms bound. All 36 CTest harnesses green on Windows. Landed 2026-08-02.

The cut gate names a green suite. BL-267.design:
FILED 2026-08-02 (Ben, immediately after confirming the BL-170 river render) — SSS priority, must design/build next. Design-owed: this entry scopes the problem and names the diagnostic + candidate directions; it does not commit to an architecture.

## The symptom, and why it is showing up now

Ben observed CPU lag this session, right after the BL-170 river render landed on top of BL-217 (checkpoint resolution), BL-208 (the history log + its generation-time genesis-chapter merge), and the Sprint 1 food-building pair. The river render in particular is a NEW always-on per-tile, per-frame cost (`src/ui/body_surface_canvas.cpp`, alongside the existing road/border/marker passes in the same per-tile loop) — every session that adds one more always-on canvas pass compounds onto the same single render thread, and world generation (six-pass tiles + nations + corporations + now the settlement-history chain BL-218/219 will extend) is a second, separate single-threaded cost paid at world-start.

## Measure before designing — do not guess where the time goes

BL-249 already built the instrument for exactly this (`src/ui/frame_stats.{hpp,cpp}`, F11 overlay, off by default): last/avg/max/1%-low frame time, broken into build/submit/present/other with ImGui vertex/draw-command counts. **NR-026 is already open asking Ben to run it** against the real app panning the full Kepler grid — that measurement is the first concrete step here, not a separate task, since it will say whether the lag is CPU-bound (sim/generation/draw-list-building) or GPU-bound (submit/present) before any architecture is chosen. BL-253 (`run_corp_strategic_step`'s O(corps x tiles) candidate scan) was already named as a growth-shape concern by the BL-250 sweep and judged "not a blocker at prototype scale" on 2026-07-31 — worth re-measuring now that the felt load is heavier and more systems are stacked on the same thread.

## Two directions, not yet chosen between

**GPU utilisation.** `docs/tech/TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md` already flags SDL3's GPU API as "available for future use ... without requiring a platform layer change" — chosen partly for this reason. Today rendering is ImGui immediate-mode plus a custom `ImDrawList` canvas (SDL3 + SDLRenderer3 backend) drawing on the order of 15,120 tiles (the full Kepler grid, per BL-249's own stated target) every frame, each with several passes (fill, landform relief, road, border, river, markers) computed on the CPU and submitted as vertex data. Open question: does "GPU utilisation" mean swapping the ImGui backend (SDLRenderer3 -> the SDL3 GPU API directly), or offloading specific per-tile computation (colour blends, river/border geometry) to a compute or vertex shader while keeping ImGui's own rendering path as-is? These are very different sizes of change.

**Multicore CPU threading.** The simulation core is explicitly deterministic (io-standing-rules.md) — no thread pool may be added to `world/*` logic without proving it cannot change iteration order or floating-point reduction order across runs. Candidate parallel-safe work, cheapest first: (a) the canvas tile loop itself is a read-only pass over `world` state per frame — computing each tile's fill/border/river geometry in parallel before a single-threaded submit to `ImDrawList` is a clean win with no simulation-determinism risk at all, since draw order can be fixed after the parallel compute; (b) per-body world generation passes are already logically independent of each other (each body's tile/nation/corp chain reads only that body's own state) and could run concurrently at world-start; (c) BL-253's per-corp strategic scan inside a tick — parallel-safe only if corp evaluation order never leaks into a shared reduction (market clearing, budget flows) in a way that changes float rounding; this one needs the most care and should be designed last, not first.

## Not yet settled

- Whether this item targets rendering only, generation only, or both — Ben's ask names both GPU and multicore, but they may resolve to different subsystems with different risk profiles, and BL-249's measurement should say which one is actually costing the frame budget before committing scope.
- Whether a thread pool / GPU compute dependency enters the build (CMakeLists.txt, FetchContent) — TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md's prototype-scope exclusions should be checked before adding one.
- Whether world-generation parallelism (per-body, at start) is in scope alongside per-frame render parallelism, or a separate follow-on — they have very different risk (once-at-startup vs every-frame) and could ship independently.

## Why design-owed rather than designed

The two directions above are real architectural forks (renderer-backend swap vs shader offload; render-loop parallelism vs generation parallelism vs simulation parallelism), each with different determinism risk and different build-system cost. Committing to one under lag pressure without the BL-249 measurement in hand would very likely solve the wrong bottleneck first.

## Measured (2026-08-02, in-session — the step this design asked for)

The BL-249 instrument gained a scripted tap (verify.frame_reset / verify.frame_csv + scripts/verify/pan_perf.lua). Nothing in src/ forces a dummy driver under --verify, so the numbers are real renderer + real vsync (this corrects NR-026's premise and frame_budget_hud.lua's stale header). 300-frame sustained pan, full Kepler grid, 1720x1080, Debug (the daily build/) vs Release (build_rel/, new Ninja tree, same pinned toolchain):

- Debug: 41-53 ms work/frame at every zoom — every frame over the 16.7 ms refresh, ~20 fps always. UI build owns 38-44 ms. /Od /RTC1 is the first cause.
- Release: 11.3-17.6 ms. Play zoom (11): ZERO frames over 16.7. Whole-grid zoom (0.9): 211/299 still over.
- Pan vs static: identical in both builds. There is no pan-specific cost; motion just exposes the constant per-frame cost.
- Sim + event pump: 0.01-0.04 ms. Submit/present: small. NEITHER fork this item posed is implicated.

VERDICT: both architectural forks declined at prototype scale. The real costs are (1) playing the unoptimised Debug binary, and (2) a flat O(all-tiles) per-frame overhead in body_surface_canvas.cpp — tile_at rebuilt per frame (logistics' body_tile_grid already caches exactly this on world, unused by the canvas), a 15k-id sort per frame, and full lens/colour work for every tile before any cull (no vertical cull exists). Both fixed by BL-268 (planetary canvas cull + cache) plus adopting build_rel/ for play. This item stays open only as the RE-MEASURE GATE: after BL-268 lands, re-run pan_perf; if the whole-grid Release residual (~155k verts of hex emission) still misses the ROADMAP budget, the follow-on is draw-list caching / coarse LOD for the zoomed-out grid — not a backend swap.

CLOSED 2026-08-07 (cut audit, Ben approved). The re-measure gate has been passed: the 2026-08-02 VERDICT declined both architectural forks, the executable half shipped as BL-268 (96712ec, complete), and the residual canvas-pass work is owned by BL-269. Nothing remains here that BL-269 does not carry.

BL-268.design:
FILED 2026-08-02, designed by measurement (see BL-267's Measured section for the full numbers; the pan_perf CSVs are reproducible via scripts/verify/pan_perf.lua).

## The mechanism (all in body_surface_canvas.cpp's draw)

1. tile_at: an unordered_map<packed rc, entity_id> of the ACTIVE body's tiles is rebuilt per frame by iterating w.tiles (ALL bodies, ~34k entries) — pure waste: logistics.hpp's body_tile_grid(w, body) already builds and caches this exact raster (grid_y*gw + grid_x -> entity, null_entity absent) on world.body_tile_index, deterministically.
2. draw_order: the 15k active-body ids are collected and std::sort'ed per frame for deterministic draw order. Tile creation (tile_generation.cpp) is rows-outer with sequential create_entity ids, so ascending-id order IS raster row-major order — iterating the cached raster reproduces today's draw order exactly, no sort needed.
3. No vertical cull: every tile computes its screen centre, resolves built/owner/lens state (several hash lookups + colour math), THEN the horizontal wrap-window (k_min/k_max) decides whether any copy is drawn; rows never cull at all. At play zoom ~2% of tiles are visible but 100% pay the per-tile work.

## The fix

- app::render (mutable world in hand) ensures body_tile_grid(m_world, active_body) is built when the active body changes; the canvas (const world&) reads world.body_tile_index directly — no const_cast, no silent fallback (assert/skip if absent).
- Replace the tile_at build + sort with row-major iteration over the cached raster, restricted to the visible row range: rows don't wrap, sc.y = view_origin.y + (1.5*hex_size*row - grid_cy)*zoom, so [r0, r1] falls out of the clip rect ± hit_r in O(1). Column culling: hoist the existing k_min/k_max wrap-window test to the TOP of the per-tile body, before the built/owner/lens work — off-screen columns cost one multiply-compare.
- The border/neighbour passes that used tile_at.find(packed) read the raster by index arithmetic instead (same null_entity semantics).
- Lens pre-passes that are lens-gated (market catchment, industry field, scarcity) stay as they are — they don't run in the default path; only the always-on costs move.

## Why pixel-identical

Draw order is unchanged (row-major == ascending id, proven from generation loop order); culled tiles contributed nothing inside the clip rect (the ±hit_r margin matches the existing horizontal logic); no colour or geometry math changes. The existing golden suite is therefore the correctness check, un-blessed.

## Verification

R1: representative golden subset passes with no --bless. R2/R3: pan_perf A/B — Release play-zoom avg work < 8 ms (ROADMAP target; baseline 11.26), Debug play-zoom < 16.7 ms (playable dev build; baseline 41.21). R4: whole-grid numbers recorded; if Release z0.9 still misses 8 ms (it will remain vertex-emission-bound, ~155k verts), file the zoomed-out LOD/draw-cache follow-on named in BL-267 rather than stretching this item.

## Scope guard

No threading, no GPU-API change, no world/* contact beyond READING the existing body_tile_index cache (built by the same logistics call the dispatch loop already uses — determinism untouched). The measurement tap (frame_stats sample/reset accessors + verify frame_reset/frame_csv/window + pan_perf.lua) lands with this item as its verification instrument.

BL-270.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-02 (Ben, via the elicitation form in the pan-perf session).

## Ben's four settlements (verbatim answers)

1. **Scope: 'Every control including chrome.'** Not just the 8 gameplay verbs, not just verbs + reading controls — literally every press: canvas clicks (select / navigate / place), the keyboard binding table (pan/zoom/lens/speed/descend/ascend, app.cpp's canvas_command table), the nav rail, ledger tabs and sub-views, the lens strip, cross-cutting selectors (body/market/resource combos), time controls, the system menu, the construction panel flow, the Selection band affordances, the comms dock, and the New World wizard's controls.
2. **Entry fields: preconditions + typed arguments** on top of the fixed A/B pair (expected_output, reason_to_select). **Deliberately excluded** (offered, not selected): cost/spend and backlog provenance — the dictionary states what a press does and why you'd press it, not what it costs (that is world-state the blackboard reports) nor which item demanded it (that is UX_QUESTIONS' axis).
3. **Store home: docs/ai/** — 'since the consumer is the AI player'. ACTIONS.json canonical + ACTIONS.md generated mirror (sibling conventions: backlog.json/BACKLOG.md, user_stories.json/USER_STORIES.md), renderer tools/session/render_actions.js modelled on render_needs_review.js.
4. **Consumer: both, in sequence.** 'Dictionary now, generation and play consume it in sequence' — word-driven procedural generation (the New World wizard via words) consumes it first, word-driven gameplay after. Ben's milestone note: 'To consider what the difficulty level will be, we need this item. That is not really one item, it's the whole process of gameplay/development.' The dictionary is the substrate; the milestone is a process, not an item (NR-034 asks where it slots in ROADMAP).

## Entry shape

Per entry: `id` (stable slug), `surface` (where the control lives, human terms), `press` (what the player physically does — click/key/drag), `args` (typed arguments, named and typed as the code takes them — e.g. build: {type: building_type, tile: entity, target: resource_type}), `preconditions` (when the press is valid — for the 8 corp verbs these MUST mirror corp_command_result's rejection semantics exactly: no_corp/not_owner/invalid/placement/funds/state), `expected_output` (A — what observably happens, stated against world/ui state, honest about durative effects like pay-as-you-build), `reason_to_select` (B — why a player or AI would choose this press over alternatives; design intent in plain words).

## Why the seams make this cheap to keep honest

The 8 gameplay verbs already have a single validated entry point (apply_corp_command, 'the contract an out-of-process policy (stage C/D) would return' — corp_command.hpp's own words) with enumerated rejections; expected_output and preconditions for those entries are TRANSCRIBED from code, not invented. The UI chrome entries are authored prose, sourced from the authority docs (CANVASES/LENSES/LAYOUT/SELECTION/STARTUP) — where a doc and the dictionary disagree, that IS the finding.

## Relationship to the siblings

Third axis, companion not replacement: user_stories.json (intent — what the player is trying to do), UX_QUESTIONS.json/BL-260 (information — what question a readout answers), ACTIONS.json (action — what a press does and why). BL-260 stays docs-only per its own settlement; ACTIONS differs in kind because its consumer is a MACHINE player as well as the designer, which is why args and preconditions are typed rather than prose-only.

## Not in scope
